p.x:
Yesterday, a new student came to our class. Her name is Emma, and she is from England. Our teacher said, "Let me introduce Emma to you all."
We all greeted her with a wai. Emma smiled and said, "Thank you!" At lunch, I sat with her. I wanted to ask her many questions about England.
In the evening, Emma had a phone call with her mum. She said goodbye to me at the school gate. Later, she sent me a funny sticker on LINE. I think we will be good friends. I can hear that her Thai is already getting better!

Communication is not only about words. A large part of what we say comes from our body language. When you nod, people know you agree. When you frown, they know something is wrong. If you shrug, it means "I don't know" or "I don't care". Your facial expression and tone of voice can show whether you are happy, angry or bored.
Eye contact is important in many Western cultures; looking away can seem rude or dishonest. In Thailand, however, people may avoid strong eye contact with older people to show respect. Even a simple gesture, such as pointing, can have different meanings in different countries.
Good communicators are also good listeners. They don't interrupt, and if they misunderstand something, they ask the speaker to repeat it or clarify what they mean. They speak clearly instead of mumbling, and they know when to whisper and when to speak up.
In social situations, small talk about the weather or food helps people relax. A sincere compliment can make someone's day. When you disagree, it's better to be polite than blunt. Today, many people send a voice message instead of typing, but the same rules apply. For many people, public speaking is the greatest challenge of all, but practice makes it easier.

Research suggests that a large proportion of communication is non-verbal, conveyed through posture, gestures and facial expressions rather than words. This is one reason why cross-cultural communication can be so challenging. A gesture that is friendly in one country may be offensive in another, and silence, which in some cultures signals respect, may be interpreted elsewhere as disapproval.
In Thailand, the concept of kreng jai, a reluctance to cause others inconvenience or embarrassment, shapes the way people communicate. Saving face is highly valued, so criticism is often expressed indirectly, and listeners must learn to read between the lines. A Western manager who expects direct feedback may completely miss a Thai colleague's polite hint that a plan is unworkable. Such miscommunication can lead to frustration on both sides.
Language itself presents obstacles. Humour and idioms are frequently lost in translation, and professionals who rely on jargon may confuse anyone outside their field. Effective communicators adapt their language to their audience, avoiding unnecessary technical terms.
One widely recommended skill is active listening. Rather than simply waiting for their turn to speak, active listeners concentrate fully, ask questions and paraphrase what they have heard to check their understanding. When giving feedback, they aim to be constructive, focusing on specific actions rather than personal criticism. These skills are valuable in every culture.
